problem: VLA-based VLN models such as StreamVLN are too slow for real-time robot use because visual tokens, including those of many history frames, dominate compute. Existing training-free pruning methods (SparseVLM, DivPrune, VisPruner) are frame-centric and ignore the spatio-temporal structure of history-conditioned VLN, so they degrade sharply at high pruning ratios.
motivation: VLN needs closed-loop, low-latency decisions on edge robots, and recent VLA navigators rely on historical observations that multiply the token count. Current and history frames play different roles: the current view needs spatial coverage, while history is largely redundant unless it relates to the current view. Training-free pruning avoids shifting pretrained representations.
key_idea: Prune current-frame tokens with an Adaptive MMR that multiplies CLS-based saliency by distinctness, then re-weight history tokens by their max similarity to the pruned current tokens and prune them with the same A-MMR.
insight: Saliency and diversity are complementary: the ablation at 70% pruning shows semantics-only lowers SR from 52.96 to 49.43 and SPL from 48.70 to 44.83, and at 90% SR falls from 48.40 to 39.53. Token merging, which helps in general VLMs, does not help in VLN (90% pruning: SR 48.40 to 46.87, SPL 36.51 to 34.43), so discarding tokens is cleaner than blurring landmarks. The gain over baselines grows with the pruning ratio.
method: Base importance: cosine similarity between the vision encoder's [CLS] token and patch tokens, min-max normalized to [0,1] (eps=1e-6), following VisPruner.
A-MMR (current frame): iteratively pick the token maximizing I_base * (1 - max cosine sim to already-selected tokens), a single unified score with no hard-coded saliency/diversity split.
Query-guided re-weighting (history): the pruned current tokens serve as queries; the relevance R of a history token is its max cosine similarity to any query.
History importance: I_final = I_base * (alpha + (1-alpha)*R) with alpha=0.5, followed by the same A-MMR selection to build a compact memory pool.
Plug-and-play integration: the selected tokens go through the unchanged projector and LLM of StreamVLN, with no training and no merging; pruning ratios of 70/80/90% keep 218/146/72 of 729 tokens.

setting.backbone: StreamVLN (pretrained VLA, frozen; pruning applied at inference)
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (current frame plus history frames); the public StreamVLN uses no depth
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions predicted as sequences of 4 (forward/turn) in VLN-CE

numbers.extra: 70% token pruning; StreamVLN without voxel pruning; H100 GPU

numbers_note: Unpruned StreamVLN (without voxel pruning) reference: R2R SR 55.74 / SPL 49.66 / OS 63.60 / NE 5.06; RxR SR 56.53 / SPL 47.26 / nDTW 64.14 / NE 5.71. Benchmarks are VLN-CE versions (mapped to R2R-CE and RxR-CE). Efficiency at 90% pruning on an RTX 4090: FPS 4.68, TFLOPs 5.61, latency 213.40 ms (unpruned 231.34 ms). Ablations were run on a different GPU and differ slightly.
results: At 90% pruning on R2R the method reaches SR 47.63 / SPL 36.36, versus VisPruner 41.16 / 29.27, SparseVLM 34.91 / 31.08 and DivPrune 27.57 / 18.55. It also wins on RxR at every ratio, and the margin widens as pruning increases. It has the best FPS (4.68) and latency (213.40 ms vs 231.34 ms unpruned). On the real Go2 with a Jetson Thor, pruning cut a 4-action inference from about 1.43 s to about 1.25 s.
limitations: Latency gains are modest (231 ms to 213 ms), and TFLOPs are no better than SparseVLM and much higher than DivPrune's.
Real-world evaluation is qualitative only, with no success rates; StreamVLN's voxel pruning is excluded, and performance still drops well below unpruned at 90% pruning.
Token merging and other design choices were tested only on R2R, and the reasons offered for the ablation results are hypotheses.
